content.title: Time capture and transparency
content.body: Start with a small pilot and explain why the organization wants to understand time use. Define who can view individual records, how entries can be corrected, and which reports will be used for planning. Test a normal work day, a meeting-heavy day, and work that spans several projects. Automated capture can reduce manual effort, but the resulting record still needs context and a fair review process.

content.title: Project context and classification
content.body: Decide how the team will associate time with clients, projects, tasks, and internal work. Use a small set of categories that people can apply consistently. Test ambiguous cases, such as switching projects mid-task or correcting an entry after the day ends. If records cannot be assigned clearly, the report may show activity without explaining what the team actually worked on.

content.title: Review and correction workflow
content.body: Run a weekly review with sample records that are complete, incomplete, and misclassified. Check whether users can correct entries and whether reviewers can understand what changed. Agree when the period is considered final and how late corrections are handled. The goal is to create a reliable operational record, not to treat every automated observation as an unquestionable fact.

content.title: Privacy and team trust
content.body: Before enabling automated capture, review the vendor's current explanation of what data is collected, when it is collected, and how it is displayed to users and administrators. Test the actual settings available to the account. Explain the intended use of the data to the team and avoid collecting more than the workflow needs. If the organization has employee monitoring policies, confirm that the setup follows them before expanding the pilot.

content.title: Reporting and data hand-off
content.body: Choose a question the team needs to answer, such as where project effort is going or which work requires better estimates. Export a representative period and compare the totals with the underlying records. Verify time zones, rounding, grouping, and the treatment of corrected entries. If the report feeds another system, test the full hand-off with a sample before relying on it.

content.title: Pricing and decision checklist
content.body: Current Timely prices, plan limits, and automated capture details are not independently verified here. Confirm the official terms for team size, projects, reports, data retention, integrations, and administration. Pilot for a complete reporting period and measure correction effort, data usefulness, user trust, and ongoing administration. No numeric editorial score is asserted until a documented assessment is completed.

content.title: Review cadence and corrections
content.body: Choose a review cadence that fits the team's work and test how a user corrects a record that has been assigned to the wrong project or task. Make sure a reviewer can understand what changed and why. Agree on who closes the period and how late corrections are handled. A transparent correction routine helps the team treat time data as a useful planning input rather than an unquestionable record.

content.title: Rollout and team trust
content.body: Introduce the workflow to a small group and explain the purpose of time collection, the people who can see reports, and how the team can raise concerns. Review the vendor's current data-handling documentation and test the account controls before expanding the pilot. Measure whether the process reduces manual entry without adding unacceptable review or administration work.

content.title: Pilot scorecard
content.body: Measure classification accuracy, manual corrections, report preparation time, user confidence, and whether the data answers a real planning question. Compare with the existing process after one complete period. If the team cannot explain a record or cannot correct it easily, adjust the process before rolling out to more people.

content.title: Implementation checklist
items: Explain the purpose and access rules.
Test a normal day and an exception case.
Agree on correction and period-close rules.

faqs.question: What should a team test first in Timely?
faqs.answer: Run a small time-tracking pilot, then review classification, corrections, report usefulness, and how users understand the collection process.

faqs.question: Are Timely's current pricing and privacy terms verified here?
faqs.answer: No. Check the vendor's current documentation and plan terms for your account and region.

faqs.question: How can a team build trust in time records?
faqs.answer: Explain the purpose, define access, allow corrections, and use records for agreed operational questions rather than unexplained surveillance.
